Got rage baited by AI overviews.

Most of my working days start with finding some good academic studies on marketing, growth, etc.

I usually run these on Google and later analyze each specific source individually.

Today it gave me this (quote below):

Generative AI Echo Chambers in SEO and Keyword Analytics

Where Published: Harvard Business School Working Knowledge / Marketing Science (2026).

The Core Issue: Marketers are heavily using AI-powered SEO and content-planning platforms (like automated SEMrush or Ahrefs workflows) to predict keyword trends and user intent.

The Insight: Because multiple competitors use the same underlying large language models (LLMs) to scan the web and generate content strategies, it creates an algorithmic feedback loop. The study terms this "semantic cannibalization." The AI models drift toward identical content clusters, flattening keyword diversity and tanking true search incrementality. The researchers proved that relying purely on LLM-driven keyword intent metrics lowers a brand's unique search footprint by 34% within six months.

Did this one catch me?
Oh yeah.

I started searching for it – but couldn't find any such study, neither on the Harvard Business School website nor in Marketing Science.

Okay, I thought – I'll try to understand where the 34% number came from.
Answer on the screenshot.

I hate this.
Building @StacysBrain to fix this.

Compared to Fusaka, Glamsterdam goes deeper and changes how Ethereum builds blocks and processes transactions.

Here are the biggest changes coming to @ethereum ↓

• ePBS: moves block-builder coordination into the protocol, so less reliance on trusted relays

• Access lists: map what each block touches, so validators can process unrelated transactions in parallel

• Gas repricing: fees match real computing and storage costs better, which makes growth more sustainable

• ETH logs: standard records for transfers and burns, easier for apps to track

• Bigger contracts: higher size limit, more room for devs to build

• Shared factory: apps can deploy at the same address across participating chains

FYI: Sepolia’s test was scheduled for today, and the Hoodi and mainnet dates are still TBD, so I’ll be watching for updates on those.

$ZIM: Own It, Don’t Trade It

The question investors keep asking is simple: when do you sell $ZIM? After all, we’ve had a run from $13 all the way to $30.

My answer: you probably don’t.

There are essentially two scenarios.

In the first, $ZIM gets acquired around the discussed $35 level. From roughly $30.50 today, that would mean about $4.50 of capital upside, with potentially another ~$5 in dividends. That puts the potential total return near 30%.

The second scenario is that the deal does not happen.

It is impossible to know how many investors currently own $ZIM mainly because of the takeover possibility. If the deal falls apart, disappointment and momentum alone could push the stock toward $27.

But that would not change the fundamental story.

By year-end, I expect $ZIM to have more than $30 per share in cash while the business remains profitable. A profitable company trading below the cash sitting on its balance sheet is not something I would panic about.

In fact, around $27 may prove to be close to a fundamental floor.

And if there is no acquisition, management will eventually have to decide what to do with all that cash.

The obvious answers are dividends, share buybacks, or both.

From my sources, significant buybacks have already been discussed with management by Israeli investors. If $ZIM remains independent, it could end up offering one of the highest dividend yields in the market, one of the largest buyback programs, or some combination of the two.

So the setup looks unusually simple.

If the buyout happens, shareholders get paid.

If it does not happen, the stock may initially fall, but investors are left owning a profitable company trading around or below its cash value, with enormous potential for capital returns.

That is why I see very little reason to sell $ZIM over the next two years.

Sometimes the best decision in investing is simply not touching the position.

By my measurement, the efficiency of intelligence output is doubling roughly every five months. 

This isn't the models getting a bit better... this is the actual amount of intelligence you get out of each unit of energy, doubling, every five months... and the doubling time is shrinking.

Nothing in human history has compounded like this. Not electricity, not the internet. And there's no playbook for it, because every institution we have was built for a world where things changed over decades.

This is what I call The Economic Singularity. Somewhere around 2030 to 2032 the machine economy starts moving faster than the instruments we use to measure it... GDP, earnings, the wage were all built for a world of scarce human labour, all pointed at an economy that no longer runs on it. 

Which means the years between now and then are the window. The whole game is to be positioned on the scarce side of the ledger before the old numbers stop meaning anything, because once the machines are running the machine economy the easy part is over. 

We have maybe five years...

The law just needs to be amended to allow what is already happening to continue happening without the side show of SS trust fund accounting tricks.

Some people are anti-AI because they can already see the downside, potentially losing their job or watching the craft they spent years learning get automated, while the promised land, curing cancer and treating diseases, still feels very far away.

AI gets incredibly useful when it has good data and a way to test whether it’s right. But biology has an enormous space of possibilities, much of the relevant data hasn’t been generated yet, and you can’t answer every question by thinking harder. At some point you have to run the experiment.

So here’s something I’d love to see someone build: a giant warehouse, basically a data center for biology, filled with lab equipment and eventually tens of thousands of robots running experiments around the clock. Liquid handlers, plate readers, microscopes, incubators, all connected to models that propose experiments, look at the results and decide what to try next.

I call the idea bounded serendipity.

A lot of discovery comes from exploring something and finding something you weren’t looking for. CRISPR came out of research into how bacteria defend themselves against viruses. RNA interference also emerged from unexpected experimental observations. These were years of careful science, but the surprise mattered. You can’t schedule the breakthrough, you can create more opportunities to encounter one.

So why wouldn’t we massively scale those opportunities? Pick a scientifically meaningful area, define what can be tested and measured reliably, then explore far more of it than a human team could. Give the models room to try unusual ideas, follow surprising results and update their understanding, with scientists deciding which questions matter and checking what the results actually mean.

Two things make me think the economics could change.

1/ Robotics. Lab automation already exists, but integrating different instruments and workflows often takes expensive custom engineering. My bet is that increasingly capable general-purpose robots, including humanoids where they make sense, could reduce how much bespoke hardware you need by using equipment designed for humans. Keep specialized machines for the tasks they do best, and use flexible robots to connect everything and handle the work between them.

We’re not yet at the point where you can buy 10,000 humanoids and expect them to run a biology lab reliably. But that’s the direction I’d bet on. Once a workflow works, you can replicate it and run shifts around the clock. Scaling that capacity could become much easier than recruiting and training thousands of lab technicians for every new facility.

2/ The data itself can be a product. Historically, the economics of an experiment often depended on whether it helped produce a valuable discovery. Now there’s another potential buyer: someone training a biology model. A well-run experiment that shows something doesn’t work can still be useful training data. A broken experiment is different, but a clean negative result tells you something about the world.

That creates a possible business model where you sell high-quality experimental datasets while also using them to build better models and pursue your own discoveries. Companies are already selling biological data for AI training, so this part is more than a hypothetical.

And parts of the loop already work. OpenAI and Ginkgo connected GPT-5 to an automated lab, tested more than 36,000 protein-synthesis reaction compositions and reported a 40% reduction in production cost. That’s a narrow result, but it’s a concrete example of a model proposing experiments, getting real measurements back and improving through iteration.

The flywheel is more experiments, more useful data, better models, smarter experiments, and data revenue funding more capacity. We’re building enormous data centers for compute. I’d love to see us build the equivalent for biology, so the promised land gets here faster. 

Bounded serendipity at industrial scale.

Looking at OpenAI releasing hundreds of mathematical results, I think we really have to lead with empathy here.

When you’ve spent years learning a craft, whether it’s writing code, creating illustrations or doing mathematics, and suddenly a lot of what you do seems to be a prompt away, of course that’s disorienting. Your craft is how you define yourself, what you’re proud of, where you find flow, sometimes the thing that gives your day meaning. It’s a huge part of your identity.

And I get how this can lead to a pretty nihilistic feeling, like you wake up one morning and think, okay, if everything can just be prompted into existence, what am I supposed to do now? What am I getting better at? What is all this effort for?

Software engineers have been grappling with this for a while, and I expect more people will experience it as AI keeps accelerating. Writing a book, creating a movie, maybe someday helping solve a disease, more and more things we’ve spent our lives learning could feel a prompt away.

I think that progress is amazing, and I’m 100% confident we’ll find harder problems to work on and new crafts to fall in love with. But knowing that intellectually doesn’t make the sense of loss disappear, especially when the change happens this fast and feels this brutal.

We can celebrate the breakthroughs and still care about the millions of people trying to figure out where they fit and what gives their life meaning in a world becoming this intelligent. “You can do more now” might be true, but people also need time to process what they feel they’ve lost.
